data.q: Which async runtime is the de facto standard for building web backends in Rust?
o: Tokio
async-std
smol
futures-executor
data.e: Tokio is the most widely used async runtime in the Rust ecosystem, powering major web frameworks like Axum, Actix-web, and Warp.

data.q: What does the `#[tokio::main]` macro expand to?
o: A function that creates a multi-threaded runtime and blocks on the async main function
A function that creates a single-threaded runtime
A function that spawns a new thread for each async task
A function that runs the async main on the current thread without a runtime
data.e: `#[tokio::main]` sets up a multi-threaded Tokio runtime by default and calls `block_on` on the async main function.

data.q: Which method is used to spawn a future onto the Tokio runtime so it runs concurrently?
o: tokio::spawn
tokio::run
tokio::execute
tokio::block_on
data.e: `tokio::spawn` returns a `JoinHandle` and schedules the future on the runtime's thread pool.

o: To run a blocking synchronous operation on a dedicated blocking thread pool
To spawn a future that blocks the current async task
To create a new OS thread for each blocking call
To block the entire runtime until the operation completes
data.e: `spawn_blocking` offloads blocking work (like file I/O or CPU-intensive calculations) to a separate thread pool so the async executor isn't stalled.

data.q: Why is `Pin<&mut Future>` required when polling a future in Rust?
o: To prevent the future from being moved in memory, which would invalidate self-referential pointers
To allow the future to be cloned across threads
To enable the future to be stored in a collection
To automatically implement the `Future` trait for the type
data.e: Async blocks and functions can create self-referential structures; `Pin` guarantees the memory address stays stable so references remain valid.

data.q: Which trait must a type implement to be used with `.await`?
o: Future
Async
Awaitable
Pollable
data.e: The `Future` trait (from `std::future` or `futures-core`) defines the `poll` method that drives async computation.

data.q: What is the role of a `Waker` in Rust's async model?
o: It notifies the executor that a task is ready to make progress and should be polled again
It wakes up the current thread from sleep
It creates a new future from a closure
It implements the `Future` trait for raw pointers
data.e: A `Waker` is passed to `poll` via `Context`; when an async operation completes (e.g., I/O ready), the waker signals the executor to reschedule the task.

o: Tokio's Mutex is async-aware: locking yields the task instead of blocking the thread
Tokio's Mutex is faster because it uses spinlocks
Tokio's Mutex does not support poisoning
Tokio's Mutex can only be used in single-threaded runtimes
data.e: `tokio::sync::Mutex::lock` returns a future, allowing the executor to run other tasks while waiting, whereas `std::sync::Mutex` blocks the OS thread.

data.q: Which runtime configuration sets the number of worker threads in Tokio?
o: `tokio::runtime::Builder::worker_threads(n)`
`tokio::runtime::Builder::max_threads(n)`
`tokio::runtime::Builder::thread_pool_size(n)`
`tokio::runtime::Builder::concurrency(n)`
data.e: The `worker_threads` method configures the number of threads in the multi-threaded scheduler's thread pool.

o: Runs multiple futures concurrently on the current task and waits for all to complete
Spawns each future on a separate thread
Runs futures sequentially in the order given
Returns the result of the first future that completes
data.e: `tokio::join!` drives multiple futures to completion concurrently within a single task, returning a tuple of their outputs.

o: Runs the async main on a single-threaded runtime
Runs the async main on a multi-threaded runtime with one worker
Disables the runtime's timer driver
Forces all spawned tasks to run on the main thread only
data.e: The `current_thread` flavor creates a single-threaded runtime where all tasks run on the same thread, useful for simpler applications or testing.

data.q: Which method on a `JoinHandle` allows you to await the result of a spawned task?
o: `.await`
`.join()`
`.result()`
data.e: `JoinHandle` implements `Future`; awaiting it yields the result of the spawned task or a `JoinError` if the task panicked.

data.q: What is the purpose of `tokio::select!` macro?
o: Races multiple futures and executes the arm of the first future that completes
Selects a random future from a list to run
Creates a new runtime with a select-based scheduler
Waits for all futures to complete and returns a vector of results
data.e: `select!` enables concurrent racing of futures, similar to `select` in Go, allowing cancellation and timeout patterns.

data.q: How can you run a future that does not implement `Send` on a multi-threaded Tokio runtime?
o: Use `tokio::task::spawn_local`
Wrap the future in `Arc<Mutex<...>>`
Use `tokio::spawn` with a `!Send` bound
It is impossible; all spawned futures must be `Send`
data.e: `spawn_local` runs a future on the current thread's local executor, avoiding the `Send` requirement needed for cross-thread work stealing.

o: A future that completes after the specified duration
A `Duration` object
A `JoinHandle` that can be awaited
An `Instant` representing the wake-up time
data.e: `sleep` returns a `Sleep` future that resolves when the deadline passes; it requires the `rt` and `time` features and a running timer driver.
